variants.reconstruction:
%n [...] ... šabiṣ | ibrī | inakkud | pagrum
#note: See @bib{RN117@206–207}: “In his transliteration of the opening lines of the tablet in Essays Pope (@bib{RN163@31}, Foster reads the end of the line as @i{úr-ba-ri} but without translating. There seem to be too many wedges present to read @akk{{giš}EREN} (so @bib{RN580@80, fn. 1}) and I have kept to the original reading of Jastrow and Clay. Tournay and Shaffer read @akk{[im-ta]-aq-qu₂-ut} (@bib{RN580@80, fn. 2}). The trace at the beginning of the line precludes this, but @akk{i#-[m]a-aq-qu₂-ut} is possible. They also sustain the old reading of the following word as @i{wa-aq-rum} but to my eyes the antepenultimate sign is @i{pa}, not @i{wa}. As I understand it, Enkidu is describing his intense physical reaction to whatever terrifying and impossible undertaking (see l. 17) Gilgameš has proposed in the lacuna.”

%n tabbiātum | ibrī || uštālipā | dâdānīya
#note: See @bib{RN117@208}: “The derivation of @i{uš-ta-li-pa} is unclear. @i{CAD} identifies the form as a III/1 perf. of @i{elēpum}, ‘to be tangled, crossed’, but comments that the meaning is uncertain. One might have expected @i{uštēlipā}. @i{AHw} enters it under a verb @i{alāpum} Št, ‘machten unbeweglich (??)’. I have translated ad hoc in the spirit of @i{CAD} and @i{AHw}. A less likely possibility is to read @i{uštallipā} < @i{šalāpum} II/1 perf., ‘to unsheath, pull out'. In the following line Enkidu complains of limpness of limbs and general weakness and it is not out of the question that this enfeeblement has affected his neck: ’sobs, my friend, have extracted the sinews from my neck’, i.e. he cannot hold his head up any more.” See also @bib{RN602@407}: “@i{uštālipā} ist ein reziproker Št₂-Stamm von @i{elēpu}: s. Rez., @i{ZA} 84 (1994) 164 f. Nr. 1.8 mit Ergänzung in @i{Verbalstämme} 121 Nr. 369. Übersetzung: ‘Klagen, mein Freund, haben meine Nackensehnen verspannt/verknotet.’”

variants.reconstruction: %n [gilgā]meš | pīšu | īpušam-ma
%n [issaqqa]ram | ana enkīdu

%n [ša qišti? | i]brī || lūliam | šadîša
#note: See @bib{RN117@210}: “Others have read at the beginning [@i{ša} @akk{{giš}}@i{er}]@i{ēnim}(eren) or even [@i{ša qišti er}]@i{ēnim} (for which room looks short, however written) but to my eyes the traces fit @i{ib-ri} better. What is restored before @i{ibrī} depends on how one construes what comes after. The reading adopted here goes back to Schott (@i{Reclam}²: “ich will ihren Berg ersteigen”). Though the verb @i{elûm} is very seldom construed with the object climbed in the accusative outside the fixed idiomatic usage of the same phrase, e.g. @i{šadâšu īli}, meaning a person disappeared-note the construction @i{ēlû šamāʾī} in l. 140 below and the repeated phrase @i{nīlû šadâ} in the late text (SB VIII 52, X 31 // 128 // 228). But there are other possibilities: (a) emend to @akk{lu-li a-<na> ša-di-ša}, (b) interpret the signs as @i{lūli aš-šadîša} (so @bib{ebeling1932review@228}; @bib{LS304@213}; @i{AHw}, p. 206; @i{CAD} E, p. 118), which would be an example, unique in this text, of the apocopated preposition prefixed to the noun, or (c) abandon the possessive suffix and boldly posit a new adverb, @i{šadîšam}, ‘mountainwards’ (cf. GAG §67g). Scott’s reading and solutions (a) and (b), with their fem. possessive, preclude the restoration of masc. @i{erēnum} and favour [@i{ša qištim}]. Solution (c) would make an anticipatory genitive of this sort unlikely and the old staple [@i{al-kam}] would then recommend itself.”

variants.reconstruction:
%n ṣiprū | šalāšā (||) manâ | ša ahīšina
#note: See @bib{RN117@212}: “A @i{ṣiprum} is typically a tapering projection like a horn or a comet’s tail (see @i{CAD} Ṣ, s.v.). Here the word occurs in a line that falls between those describing the daggers’ blades and pommels and are qualified as being ‘of the blades’ sides’. The reference can only be to a projecting crossguard that keep the user’s hand from slipping on to the blade (so already Labat: ‘crête de leur garde’). Good examples of blades furnished with such projections are the famous gold daggers from the royal cemetery at Ur. The curved guard projects out from the blade on either side in the manner of two horns or crests (photographs: Woolley, @i{UE} II, pls. 155, 157).”

variants.reconstruction:
%n [i]hzū (|) patrī | šalāšā (|) manâ | hurāṣa
#note: See @bib{RN117@212}: “A similarly composite dagger, with a blade of hard metal and @i{iḫzu}s of gold, is reported by Aššurbanipal: @i{patar}(gír) @i{parzilli}(an.bar) @i{šib-bi šá iḫ-zu-šú ḫurāṣu}(kù.sig₁₇), ‘an iron dagger (worn in) the belt, whose mountings are gold’ (V @i{R} 2 ii 12, ed. @bib{RN1743@14}). The word @i{iḫzu} is conventionally understood as a mounting for decorative inlay. In a dagger @i{iḫzu}s are most easily imagined as forming the main component of the hilt’s pommel, since soft metal and decoration are most appropriate to this part of a weapon.”

#note: See @bib{RN117@213–214}: “Elsewhere in literary OB the terminative @i{qātiš-šunu} would be spelled @i{qá-ti-iš-šu-nu} (e.g. @bib{thureaudangin1925hymne@170, 14}: @i{qá-ti-iš-ša}; @bib{groneberg1981philologische@110}, v 26: @i{qá-ti-iš-šu}; p. 127, viii 8: @i{qá-ti-iš-ša}; cf. @bib{groneberg1978terminativ@24–6}, for attestations of terminative+pron. suffixes on other words. Note that example B I d5 @i{ra-i-mi-iš-sa} is a misprint for @i{ra-i-mi-iš-ša}). The present orthography is exactly that which was current in the Sargonic period (cf. 214 @akk{qa₂-ti-is₂(IŠ)-su} = @i{qātiš-šu} in e.g. @i{PBS} V 36 rev. iii’ 17; @i{UET} I 275 iii 5; both Narām-Sîn), and is thus to be explained as an archaic spelling. In the Pennsylvania and Yale tablets other spellings of this type, VŠ+SV, are used where /ss/ is a development of /š+š of pronominal suffix/ (see above, fn. 5).” See also @bib{RN2651@11a}: “Jn the break, perhaps, a form of @i{tamāḫu}”

%n [išša]knū | ippušū | alākam
#note: See @bib{RN117@214}: “The beginning of the line has provoked different solutions: some restore @akk{[um-m]a-nu} (following @bib{LS304@214}), others [@i{ina sū}]@i{qim} (following von Soden, @i{Reclam}², p. 37, ‘auf der Straße'). To my eyes neither fits the traces, and I prefer a solution which provides a climax to the preparations (cf. @bib{westenholz_gilgamesh_1997@156, 185}: ‘da de var parate’).”

%n [eṭlūtu]m? | ukarrabū | gilgāmeš
#note: See @bib{RN117@214}: “In the absence of a preposition before Gilgameš, @akk{u₂-GA-ra-bu} is hardly @i{qurrubum}, ‘to approach’ (@bib{RN272}). Despite the contrasting spelling of @i{i-ka-ra-bu-šu} in l. 247 the verb of the present line must also be a form of @i{karābu}. The spelling represents a survival of third-millennium practice. The verb takes the present tense because, as a verbum dicendi, it introduces speech.”

%n [...] ... | tuttēr | ana libbi (|) āli
#note: See @bib{RN117@214}: “Von Soden took the verb as II/2 preterite, restored @akk{[ina m]a-ti}, and translated ‘Wann würdest du zurückgebracht in die Stadt?’, but with the comment ‘es ist nicht klar, … was damit gemeint wird’ (@bib{LS304@214}; see similarly Reclam⁴⁻⁵ but note Reclam²: ‘bring zurück zur Stadt!’). Others have translated similarly (Dalley, Hecker), or as if the verb was a simple I/1 present, either as a question (Heidel, Labat, Bottéro, and, restoring @akk{[im-m]a-ti}, @bib{RN580@95, fn. 98}), a wish (Speiser) or a prediction (Pettinato). The verb is unsuited to a question relating to Gilgameš’s anticipated return--unless it is future perfect, i.e. II/1 transitive and notably lacks the ventive ending that would be expected if it referred to the hero’s homecoming. Apart from the problems raised by @i{tuttēr}, the first word is also open to doubt: Clay’s copy did not suggest that the broken sign could be @i{ma} and to my eyes it is more like @i{ne}. Rather than an interrogative, the broken word might be the object of transitive @i{tuttēr}.”

#note: See @bib{RN117@215}: “The opinion of Oppenheim, that @i{kīma ṣeḫrim} is simply a way of saying ‘quickly’ (@bib{RN729@33, fn. 2}; cf. @bib{RN2165@269, fn. 103}), must be modified in the light of the evidence of the OB love incantations from Isin, which reveal that @i{ernittam kīma ṣeḫrim kašādum} is a stock image: @akk{a-di ki-ma ṣe₂-eh-ri-im e-le-eq-qu₂-u₂ er-ni-[it-ti]}, ‘until, like a child, I obtain my own way’ (@bib{wilcke1985liebesbeschwoerungen@204, 111}); cf. also @akk{am-mi-ni ki-ma ṣe-eh-ri-im la-hi-im er-ni-it-ta-ka le-em-ne₂-et}, ‘why, like a tiny child, is your (insistence on getting) what you want so annoying?’ (ibid., p. 200, 54). In Wilcke’s words, ‘es ist vielmehr das Bild des hartnäckig entgegen jeder Vernunft auf der Erfüllung seiner Wünsche bestehenden Kindes gemeint’ (ibid., p. 207).” See also @bib{RN602@408}: “Für den Vergleich @i{kīma ṣeḫri} s. @i{Bildersprache} S. 62 Nr. 16; danach ist eine Wurzel des Vergleichs die Deutung des in Z. 263 genannten Namens Lugalbanda als „kleiner König“.”

variants.reconstruction:
%n ina nārim | ša huwāwa | ša tuṣammaru
#note: See @bib{RN117@215}: “266–7. The ‘river of Ḫuwawa’ is otherwise unknown and does not quite ring true as the object of Gilgameš’s strivings: his stated ambitions are to defeat Ḫuwawa by force of arms and to fell the cedars under his protection. One thus has some sympathy for those who prefer @i{nârum}, ‘to slay’, to @i{nārum}, ‘river’, but Speiser’s rendering, ‘after the slaying of Ḫuwawa’, mistranslates @i{ina nârim}, which as an infinitive construction would mean ‘while slaying, by slaying'. As the text stands this would be a curious way of inciting Gilgameš to stand awash in Ḫuwawa’s blood and accordingly I have stayed with ‘river'. But it may be that we are misled by a defective text, for l. 267 @i{misi šēpīka} is unusually short for a poetic line.” Note, in addition, the absence of trochaic ending in l. 266.

variants.reconstruction:
%n [(...) aš]ar | taštaknu | epuš | alākam
#note: See @bib{RN117@215}: “Von Soden read @akk{[ki]-ma ta-aš-tan-nu} < @i{šanānum} I/2, ‘so, wie du gekämpfst hat’ (@bib{LS304@215}; cf. Speiser: ‘[Since] contend thou wilt’), and this decipherment has found its way into his syllabary as a parade example of OB use of the value @i{tan} (@bib{AkkSyll@33}; also @i{AHw}, p. 1162; @i{CAD} Š/1, p. 369). However, such a reading is very doubtful. First, the traces do not allow @akk{[ki]-ma}. Second, the third sign of the verb is not certainly @i{tan}. There is no example of the syllabic value @i{tan} elsewhere in the Pennsylvania and Yale tablets (the only time the syllable is written it is spelled @i{ta-an}: OB II 204), but when the @akk{KAL} sign is used, on occasion for @i{eṭlum} (guruš: II 147, 193, III 283), it does not match the sign in question here, which has too many vertical wedges to be read so. Instead it compares favourably with the certain @i{ták} in l. 188. But there remains a problem of meaning: given that @i{taštaknu} should be transitive, whether I/1 or I/2, what is its object? With some hesitation I assume that the phrase is an abbreviation of the idiom @i{ašar pānīka taštaknu}.” See also the restoration @akk{[iš-t]u} proposed by @bib{RN2651@11b}: “[sin]ce you have already been equipped, begin the journey!”
